highlights.prose:
An explicit exponent (a remark, not a correction). The paper states no exponent
for its running time. Theorem 1.1.1 says “quasipolynomial”, that is, exp((log n)O(1) ). A
formalization of the paper in Lean 4 with Mathlib proves more: one program on a random
5
access machine solves String Isomorphism within 2c(log2 N +2) steps on every input of length
N , for an absolute constant c (Explicit.theorem 1 1 1 exponent5). The exponent 5 comes
2
from the paper’s own recurrences. Eq. (6) and Eq. (74) bound the cost by q(n)O(log n) , where
q(n) is the multiplicative cost of one significant reduction. The cost of Section 9 as proved
is q(n) = exp(O(log3 n)): there are O(log n) turns of Split-or-Johnson, and each applies the
Design Lemma at cost nO(log n) . So the total is exp(O(log5 n)). The other factor of Eq. (6),
(ℓ(n)!)O(log n) , is smaller: ℓ(n) is at most (log n)3 , so this factor is exp(O(log4 n log log n)).
The text of the paper is not changed for this.

Proposition 2.2.6. (a) [Kernel of action] Let Ω and Γ be sets, G ≤ S(Ω), and let φ :
G → S(Γ) be a G-action on Γ. Then one can, in polynomial time, determine ker(φ),
the kernel of this action.
(b) [Lifting] Let, in addition, τ ∈ S(Γ). Then one can, in polynomial time, determine the
set φ−1 (τ ) (which is either empty or a coset of ker(φ) in G).

highlights.prose:
Definition 2.3.1. A k-ary relation on the set Ω is a subset R ⊆ Ω k . We say that the
arity of R is k. A relational structure X = (Ω; R) consists of Ω, the set of vertices, and
R = (R1 , . . . , Rr ), a list of relations on Ω. We write Ω = V (X). We say that X is a k-ary
relational structure if each Ri is k-ary.

that 0 ≤ defect(G) < 1.

defect(Aut(X)).

highlights.prose:
Observation 2.3.17 (Computing symmetricity and symmetry defect). We observed that
candidate isomorphisms of explicit relational structures can be tested in polynomial time
(Prop. 2.3.6). In particular, candidate automorohisms can be tested in polynomial time.
Consequently, one can find the twin equivalence classes in polynomial time (test each
transposition). Therefore, the symmetricity and the symmetry defect of explicit relational
structures can also be computed in polynomial time. A similar observation holds for explicit
hypergraphs (see Obs. 2.5.8).

R(x) = {y ∈ Ω | (x, y) ∈ R} for the set of out-neighbors of x. Note that R− (x) is the set of
in-neighbors of x.

highlights.prose:
Definition 2.4.3. A digraph (directed graph) is a pair X = (Ω, E) where E ⊆ Ω × Ω is a
binary relation on Ω. We say that Ω is the set of vertices and E is the set of edges of X.
Vertex u is the tail and vertex v the head of the edge (u, v). The edge emanates from its tail
and is absorbed by its head. We call E the adjacency relation. If (u, v) ∈ E, we say that u is
adjacent to v. If we reverse every edge, we obtain the digraph X − = (Ω, E − ).

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Definition 2.4.17 (Walks, strong components) (PDF p. 23) — Definition 2.4.17.  "A *walk of length `t ≥ 0`* in the digraph `X = (Ω, E)` is a sequence `(u₀,…,u_t)` of vertices such that `(∀ i ≥ 1)((u_{i-1}, u_i) ∈ E)`."
highlights.prose:
Definition 2.4.17 (Walks, strong components). A walk of length t ≥ 0 in the digraph
X = (Ω, E) is a sequence (u0 , . . . , ut ) of vertices such that (∀i ≥ 1)((ui−1 , ui ) ∈ E). We
say that this walk starts at u0 and ends at ut . We say that vertex v is accessible from
vertex u if there exists a walk that starts at u and ends at v. We say that u and v are
mutually accessible if each is accessible from the other. Mutual accessibility is an equivalence
relation on Ω; its equivalence classes are called the strong components of X. We say that
X is strongly connected if every vertex is accessible from every vertex, i. e., there is just one
strong component.

and Xi are oriented.

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Observation 3.2.3 (PDF p. 31) — Observation 3.2.3.  "Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` be a permutation group.  The orbital configuration `X(G)` is primitive if and only if the group `G` is primitive."
highlights.prose:
Observation 3.2.3. Let G ≤ S(Ω) be a permutation group. The orbital configuration
X(G) is primitive if and only if the group G is primitive, provided |Ω| ≥ 2.F11 X(G) is a
clique configuration if and only if G is doubly transitive. Therefore X(G) is a UPCC if and
only if G is uniprimitive (primitive but not doubly transitive).
A graph theoretic study of UPCCs was initiated by the author [Ba81] in 1980, with an
immediate contribution by Viktor Zemlyachenko [ZKT] (see [Ba81, updated version]). This
line of work reached great depth in a recent major paper by Sun and Wilmes [SuW] (2015).
UPCCs play an important role in the study of GI as the obstacles to natural combinatorial
partitioning. One of the main technical contributions of this paper is that we overcome this
obstacle at a logarithmic multiplicative cost (Section 9).

vertex colors i and j (so Rk ⊆ Ωi × Ωj ; in particular, the vertices have two colors).

S ⊆ [r]∗ of finite strings of colors (strings over the alphabet [r]), we say that vertex y is
accessible from vertex x along S if (∃w ∈ S)(y is accessible from x along a walk of color
composition w). We write S(x) to denote the set of vertices accessible from x along S.

highlights.prose:
Corollary 3.3.13 (Accessibility set). Given a (not necessarily finite) set S ⊆ [r]∗ of finite

highlights.prose:
Lemma 3.4.6 (Neighborhood of connected component of constituent). Let Ω1 and Ω2 be
two distinct vertex-color classes; let i = c(z) for z ∈ Ωi (i = 1, 2). Let B1 , . . . , Bm be the
connected components of the homogeneous constituent digraph X3 = (Ω1 , R3 ) in Ω1 and let
X4 = (Ω1 , Ω2 ; R4 ) be a bipartite constituent between Ω1 and Ω2 (so R4 ⊆ Ω1 × Ω2 ). For
j = 1, . . . , m let Mj denote the set of R4 -out-neighbors of Bj , i. e., the set of vertices v ∈ Ω2
such that there exists w ∈ Bj such that c(w, v) = 4. Then |M1 | = · · · = |Mm |.

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Definition 3.4.26 (PDF p. 41) — Definition 3.4.26.  "A *BIBD* is a possibly degenerate BIBD satisfying `λ ≥ 1`."
highlights.prose:
Definition 3.4.26. A possibly degenerate BIBD with parameters (v, b, r, k, λ) is an r-regular
k-uniform hypergraph with v vertices and b not necessarily distinct edges such that each pair
of vertices belongs to exactly λ “blocks” (edges) where k, r ≥ 1 and k < v; the latter is the
“incompleteness” condition.
A BIBD is a possibly degerenate BIBD satisfying λ ≥ 1.
Note that v ≥ 1 (in fact, v ≥ 2 because v > k ≥ 1) and therefore b ≥ r ≥ 1.
For a degenerate BIBD we have λ = 0, so each block is a singleton, i. e., k = 1 and
therefore b = rv ≥ v.

highlights.prose:
Definition 5.4.3 (Configuration). We say that the k-ary relational structure X is a k-ary
configuration if the following hold:
(i) the Ri partition Ω k and all the Ri are nonempty;
(ii) if c(x1 , . . . , xk ) = c(x′1 , . . . , x′k ) then (∀i, j ≤ k)(xi = xj ⇐⇒ x′i = x′j );
(iii) (∀π ∈ Sk )(∀i ≤ r)(∃j ≤ r)(Riπ = Rj ).
Here Rπ denotes the relation Rπ = {(x1π , . . . , xkπ ) | (x1 , . . . , xk ) ∈ R}.
We call r the rank of the configuration. We note that the t-skeleton of a configuration of
rank r is a configuration of rank ≤ r (we keep only one copy of identical relations).
Vertex colors are the colors of the diagonal elements: c(x) = c(x, . . . , x). We say that
the configuration X is homogeneous if all vertices have the same color. We note that the
s-skeleton of a k-ary homogeneous configuration is homogeneous.

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Definition 7.1.1 (PDF p. 62) — Definition 7.1.1.  *"A colored partition of a set `Ω` is a coloring of the elements of `Ω` along with a partition of each color class."*
highlights.prose:
Definition 7.1.1. A colored partition of a set Ω is a coloring of the elements of Ω along
with a partition of each color class. We say that this is a colored equipartition if all blocks
within the same color class have equal size. Given a colored partition Π, let C1 , . . . , Cr be
the color classes and {Bij | 1 ≤ j ≤ ki } be the blocks of Ci . We say that Π is admissible if
for each color class Ci of size |Ci | ≥ 2, all the blocks of Ci have size |Bij | ≥ 2. (Bij = Ci is
permitted.) Let ρ(Π) = maxi,j |Bij |. For 0 < α ≤ 1, a colored α-partition is an admissible
colored partition Π such that ρ(Π) ≤ αn where n = |Ω|.

highlights.prose:
Theorem 8.1.2 (Design lemma). Let 1/2 ≤ α < 1 be a threshold parameter. Let X = (Ω, R)
be a k-ary relational structure with n = |Ω| vertices, 2 ≤ k ≤ n/2, and symmetry defect
≥ 1 − α. Then in time nO(k) we can find a value ℓ ≤ k − 1 and a string ⃗x = x1 . . . xℓ ∈ Ω⟨ℓ⟩
of ℓ distinct vertices such that by individualizing each xj we obtain either
(a) a canonical coloring of Ω with no dominant color, or
(b) a canonical coloring of Ω and a nontrivial canonical equipartition of the dominant color
class, or
(c) a canonical coloring of Ω and a canonically embedded uniprimitive coherent configuration
(UPCC) whose vertex set is the dominant color class.
Canonicity in the above statements is relative to ⃗x.

highlights.prose:
Theorem 8.1.5 (Design lemma, rephrased). Let 1/2 ≤ α < 1 be a threshold parameter.
Let X = (Ω, R) be a k-ary relational structure with n = |Ω| vertices, 2 ≤ k ≤ n/2, and
symmetry defect ≥ 1 − α. Then in time nO(k) we can find a value ℓ ≤ k − 1 and a string
⃗x = x1 . . . xℓ ∈ Ω⟨ℓ⟩ of ℓ distinct vertices such that by individualizing each xj we obtain either
(i) a canonical coloring of Ω with no dominant color, or
(ii) a canonical (classical) coherent configuration X∗ on vertex set Ω such that the subconfiguration induced on the dominant vertex-color class of X∗ is not a clique.
Canonicity in the above statements is relative to ⃗x.

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Remark 10.1.2 (PDF p. 83) — **Remark 10.1.2**, §10.1, the derivation:
highlights.prose:
Remark 10.1.2. A group H is perfect if H ′ = H (where H ′ = [H, H] denotes the commutator subgroup of H). Pálfy points out that the following result appears as Lemma 2.8 in
[Me].
Lemma 10.1.3 (Meierfrankenfeld). Let G be a finite group and N ◁ G such that G/N is
perfect. Then there exists a unique subnormal subgroup R of G which is minimal with respect
to G = RN .
Lemma 10.1.1 follows from this ⋂︁result. Indeed, observe that if Mi N = G for all i then
R ≤ Mi for all i and therefore R ≤ i Mi = 1, contradicting the equation RN = G.
We believe, though, that Lemma 10.1.1 must have been folklore decades before this 1995
reference.

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Definition 11.1.10 (Straight-line program) (PDF p. 93) — Definition 11.1.10 (Straight-line program), §11.1.
highlights.prose:
Definition 11.1.10 (Straight-line program). Given a group G by a list S of generators, a
straight-line program of length ℓ in G is a sequence of length ℓ of elements of G such that
each element in the sequence is either one of the generators or is a product of two elements
earlier in the sequence or is the inverse of an element earlier in the sequence. We say that
the straight-line program computes a set T of elements if the elements of T appear in the
sequence and are marked as belonging to T . A subgroup is computed if a set of generators
of the subgroup is computed. A coset is computed if the corresponding subgroup and a coset
representative are computed.

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson (PDF p. 94) — §11.3, Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson, **step 1**.
highlights.prose:
Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson
Input: group G ≤ S(Ω), strings x, y : Ω → Σ
Output: IsoG (x, y) or updated Ω, G, x, y, G transitive, with set B of blocks on which G acts
as Johnson group G ≤ S(B)
1. if G ≤ Aut(x) then
if x = y then return IsoG (x, y) = G, exit
else return IsoG (x, y) = ∅, exit
2. if |G| < C0 for some absolute constant C0 then compute IsoG (x, y) by brute force, exit
3. if G intransitive then apply Chain Rule
4. (: G transitive :) Find minimal block system B. Let m = |B|. Let G ≤ S(B) be the
induced G-action on B and N the kernel of the G → G epimorphism (: G is a primitive
group :)
5. if |G| < m1+log2 m then reduce G to N via imprimitive Luks reduction

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Remark 12.0.2 (PDF p. 97) — §12, **Remark 12.0.2**.
highlights.prose:
Remark 12.0.2. H does not need to be a permutation group. What we need is that H
permit constructive membership testing, i. e., for any list of elements τ1 , . . . , τk , ρ ∈ H we
should be able to efficiently decide whether ρ ∈ K where K is the subgroup generated by
the τi , and if the answer is affirmative, to produce a straight-line program that constructs ρ
from the τi (see Def. 11.1.10). Constructive membership testing can be done, for instance,
for matrix groups over finite fields of odd characteristic in quantum polynomial time [BaBS].

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Definition 12.0.3 (PDF p. 97) — §12, **Definition 12.0.3**.
highlights.prose:
Definition 12.0.3. A subcoset of a group G is a coset of a subgroup. Let H ≤ G be groups
and τ ∈ G. We say that the subset S ⊆ Hτ is a set of coset generators of Hτ if Hτ is the
smallest subcoset of G containing S. (Note that any intersection of subcosets of G is either
empty or a subcoset; so every subset of G generates a subcoset of G.)

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Certificate of fullness. (PDF p. 101) — §13.1, **Certificate of fullness**.
highlights.prose:
Certificate of fullness. A certificate of fullness of the test set T ⊂ Γ is a permutation
group K(T ) ≤ S(Ω) such that
(i) K(T )T ≥ A(T )

and

(ii) K(T ) ≤ AutGT (x).
Note that K(T ) represents an easily (polynomial-time) verifiable proof of fullness of T .
Our ability to find K(T ), the certificate of fullness, may be surprising because it means
that from a local start (that may take only a small segment of x into account), we have to
build up global automorphisms (automorphisms of the full string x). Our ability to do so
critically depends on the “Unaffected Stabilizers Lemma” (Thm. 10.3.5).

highlights.rationale: Formalizes Remark 16.1.1 (PDF p. 116) — **Theorem 2.2.4 (a)** (Degree of transitivity), §2.2.2.
highlights.prose:
Remark 16.1.1. Stronger bounds hold on the degree of transitivity. Under CFSG, we have
t ≤ 5, and in fact t ≤ 3 if k ≥ 25. Moreover, Wielandt [Wi2] (see [DiM, Thm. 7.3A]) has
shown that assuming only Schreier’s Hypothesis, one can prove t ≤ 7. So 6 individualizations
(rather than 3 ln k individualizations) suffice in the above argument if we are willing to assume
Schreier’s Hypothesis. (Note also that if we do encounter a 7-transitive group that is not a
giant, we shall have found an explicit counterexample to Schreier’s Hypothesis and thereby
to CFSG, an impressive by-product.)

highlights.prose:
Definition 2.3.1. A k-ary relation on the set Ω is a subset R ⊆ Ω k . We say that the
arity of R is k. A relational structure X = (Ω; R) consists of Ω, the set of vertices, and
R = (R1 , . . . , Rr ), a list of relations on Ω. We write Ω = V (X). We say that X is a k-ary
relational structure if each Ri is k-ary.

highlights.prose:
Proposition 2.3.6 (Testing candidate isomorphism). Given two explicit relational structures
X = (Ω, R) and X′ = (Ω′ , R′ ) and a bijection σ : Ω → Ω′ , one can decide in linear time
whether σ ∈ Iso(X, X′ ). In particular, given an explicit relational structure X = (Ω, R) and a
permutation σ ∈ S(Ω), one can decide in linear time whether σ ∈ Aut(X).

quantity |Ω| − s(G). The relative symmetry defect of G is defect(G) = 1 − s(G)/|Ω|. Note
that 0 ≤ defect(G) < 1.

quantity |Ω| − s(G). The relative symmetry defect of G is defect(G) = 1 − s(G)/|Ω|. Note
that 0 ≤ defect(G) < 1.

highlights.prose:
Notation 2.4.1 (In-neighbors, out-neighbors). Let R ⊆ Ω × Ω be a binary relation on the
set Ω. The inverse relation R− is defined as R− = {(y, x) | (x, y) ∈ R}. If (x, y) ∈ R,
we say that y is an out-neighbor of x and x is an in-neighbor of y. For x ∈ Ω we write
R(x) = {y ∈ Ω | (x, y) ∈ R} for the set of out-neighbors of x. Note that R− (x) is the set of
in-neighbors of x.

highlights.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 2.4.17 (Walks, strong components) (PDF p. 23) — Accessibility (Def. 2.4.17) is the reflexive-transitive closure of adjacency. highlights.prose:
Definition 2.4.17 (Walks, strong components). A walk of length t ≥ 0 in the digraph
X = (Ω, E) is a sequence (u0 , . . . , ut ) of vertices such that (∀i ≥ 1)((ui−1 , ui ) ∈ E). We
say that this walk starts at u0 and ends at ut . We say that vertex v is accessible from
vertex u if there exists a walk that starts at u and ends at v. We say that u and v are
mutually accessible if each is accessible from the other. Mutual accessibility is an equivalence
relation on Ω; its equivalence classes are called the strong components of X. We say that
X is strongly connected if every vertex is accessible from every vertex, i. e., there is just one
strong component.

highlights.prose:
Definition 2.4.17 (Walks, strong components). A walk of length t ≥ 0 in the digraph
X = (Ω, E) is a sequence (u0 , . . . , ut ) of vertices such that (∀i ≥ 1)((ui−1 , ui ) ∈ E). We
say that this walk starts at u0 and ends at ut . We say that vertex v is accessible from
vertex u if there exists a walk that starts at u and ends at v. We say that u and v are
mutually accessible if each is accessible from the other. Mutual accessibility is an equivalence
relation on Ω; its equivalence classes are called the strong components of X. We say that
X is strongly connected if every vertex is accessible from every vertex, i. e., there is just one
strong component.

highlights.prose:
Observation 2.5.8. Candidate isomorphisms (and therefore automorphisms) of explicit6
hypergraphs can be tested in polynomial time (cf. Prop. 2.3.6). In particular, one can find
the twin equivalence classes of an explicit hypergraph in polynomial time. Consequently,
the symmetry defect of a hypergraph can also be computed in polynomial time. (A similar
observation was made regarding explicit relational structures, Obs. 2.3.17).

highlights.prose:
Proposition 2.5.11. Let H = (V, E) be a nonempty, regular, d-uniform hypergraph. Let
S ⊆ V . Let α = |S|/|V |. Then there is an edge Ei ∈ E such that |Ei ∩ S| ≥ αd.

highlights.prose:
Terminology 3.1.3. Axiom (i) says that (∀i)(either Ri ⊆ diag(Ω) or Ri ∩ diag(Ω) = ∅).
In the former case we say that i is a diagonal color and Xi is a diagonal constituent; in the
latter case we speak of an off-diagonal color and constituent.
Axiom (ii) says that c(x, y) determines c(y, x), i. e., (∀i)(∃j)(Rj = Ri− ). We write j = i−
if Rj = Ri− . If i is an off-diagonal color and i− = i (i. e., Ri− = Ri ) then we say that the color
i and the constituent Xi are undirected ; otherwise (in this case Ri ∩ Ri− = ∅), we say that i
and Xi are oriented.

highlights.prose:
Observation 3.2.3. Let G ≤ S(Ω) be a permutation group. The orbital configuration
X(G) is primitive if and only if the group G is primitive, provided |Ω| ≥ 2.F11 X(G) is a
clique configuration if and only if G is doubly transitive. Therefore X(G) is a UPCC if and
only if G is uniprimitive (primitive but not doubly transitive).
A graph theoretic study of UPCCs was initiated by the author [Ba81] in 1980, with an
immediate contribution by Viktor Zemlyachenko [ZKT] (see [Ba81, updated version]). This
line of work reached great depth in a recent major paper by Sun and Wilmes [SuW] (2015).
UPCCs play an important role in the study of GI as the obstacles to natural combinatorial
partitioning. One of the main technical contributions of this paper is that we overcome this
obstacle at a logarithmic multiplicative cost (Section 9).

Corollary 3.3.7 (Constituents: homogeneous or bipartite). For k ≤ r, the constituent
digraph Xk = (Ω(k), Rk ) is either
(i) (homogeneous case) a biregular digraph with vertex set Ω(k) = Ωi for some vertex color
i (in particular, all vertices of Xk have the same color), or
(ii) (bipartite case) a semiregular bipartite graph of the form (Ωi , Ωj ; Rk ) for some distinct
vertex colors i and j (so Rk ⊆ Ωi × Ωj ; in particular, the vertices have two colors).

Lemma 3.4.25 (Large clique lemma). Let X = (Ω, c) be a coherent configuration. Let
Ω1 , . . . , Ωs be the vertex-color classes. Assume |Ω1 | > |Ωi | for all i ≥ 2 and Ω1 induces a
clique configuration in X. Then Ω1 is a twin equivalence class in X. In particular, all links
between color 1 and the other vertex colors are trivial. Moreover, the symmetry defect of X
is 1 − |Ω1 |/|Ω|.

highlights.prose:
Definition 3.4.26. A possibly degenerate BIBD with parameters (v, b, r, k, λ) is an r-regular
k-uniform hypergraph with v vertices and b not necessarily distinct edges such that each pair
of vertices belongs to exactly λ “blocks” (edges) where k, r ≥ 1 and k < v; the latter is the
“incompleteness” condition.
A BIBD is a possibly degerenate BIBD satisfying λ ≥ 1.
Note that v ≥ 1 (in fact, v ≥ 2 because v > k ≥ 1) and therefore b ≥ r ≥ 1.
For a degenerate BIBD we have λ = 0, so each block is a singleton, i. e., k = 1 and
therefore b = rv ≥ v.

a k-ary configuration if the following two axioms hold. For all ⃗x, ⃗y ∈ Ωk and τ ∈ Mk , if

(i)

of τ (⃗x ) for any given τ .

highlights.prose:
Definition 7.1.1. A colored partition of a set Ω is a coloring of the elements of Ω along
with a partition of each color class. We say that this is a colored equipartition if all blocks
within the same color class have equal size. Given a colored partition Π, let C1 , . . . , Cr be
the color classes and {Bij | 1 ≤ j ≤ ki } be the blocks of Ci . We say that Π is admissible if
for each color class Ci of size |Ci | ≥ 2, all the blocks of Ci have size |Bij | ≥ 2. (Bij = Ci is
permitted.) Let ρ(Π) = maxi,j |Bij |. For 0 < α ≤ 1, a colored α-partition is an admissible
colored partition Π such that ρ(Π) ≤ αn where n = |Ω|.

highlights.prose:
Theorem 8.1.2 (Design lemma). Let 1/2 ≤ α < 1 be a threshold parameter. Let X = (Ω, R)
be a k-ary relational structure with n = |Ω| vertices, 2 ≤ k ≤ n/2, and symmetry defect
≥ 1 − α. Then in time nO(k) we can find a value ℓ ≤ k − 1 and a string ⃗x = x1 . . . xℓ ∈ Ω⟨ℓ⟩
of ℓ distinct vertices such that by individualizing each xj we obtain either
(a) a canonical coloring of Ω with no dominant color, or
(b) a canonical coloring of Ω and a nontrivial canonical equipartition of the dominant color
class, or
(c) a canonical coloring of Ω and a canonically embedded uniprimitive coherent configuration
(UPCC) whose vertex set is the dominant color class.
Canonicity in the above statements is relative to ⃗x.

highlights.prose:
Lemma 8.3.1 (Non-clique lemma). Let 1/2 ≤ α ≤ 1 be a threshold parameter. Let X =
(Ω, R) be a k-ary coherent configuration with n = |Ω| vertices, 2 ≤ k ≤ n/2, and symmetry
defect ≥ 1 − α. Assume X has a dominant vertex-color class C, so |C| > αn. The there exists
a string ⃗x ∈ Ω⟨≤k−1⟩ such that either
(a) C \ supp(⃗x ) is not homogeneous under the coloring c⃗x (not all elements get the same
color), or
(b) ℓ(⃗x ) ≤ k − 2 and the classical coherent configuration induced by the 2-skeleton (X⃗x )(2) on
the set C \ supp(⃗x ) is not a clique.

bipartite graph with |V1 | ≥ 2 and let 2/3 ≤ α < 1 be a threshold parameter. Assume |V2 | <
α|V1 |. Assume moreover that the symmetry defect of X on V1 is at least 1 − α. Then at
quasipolynomial multiplicative cost we can find either
(a) a canonical colored α-partition of V1 , or
(b) a canonically embedded nontrivial Johnson scheme on a subset of V1 of size ≥ α|V1 |.
(The time bounds do not depend on α.)

Let X = (Ω, R) be a k-ary relational structure with n vertices, 2 ≤ k ≤ n/4, and relative
strong symmetry defect > 1 − α. Then at a multiplicative cost of q(n)nO(k) , where q(n) is a
quasipolynomial function, we can find either
(a) a canonical colored α-partition of the vertex set, or
(b) a canonically embedded nontrivial Johnson scheme on a subset W ⊆ Ω of size |W | ≥ αn.
(The time bounds do not depend on α.)

highlights.prose:
Definition 11.1.10 (Straight-line program). Given a group G by a list S of generators, a
straight-line program of length ℓ in G is a sequence of length ℓ of elements of G such that
each element in the sequence is either one of the generators or is a product of two elements
earlier in the sequence or is the inverse of an element earlier in the sequence. We say that
the straight-line program computes a set T of elements if the elements of T appear in the
sequence and are marked as belonging to T . A subgroup is computed if a set of generators
of the subgroup is computed. A coset is computed if the corresponding subgroup and a coset
representative are computed.

Theorem 11.2.1. Let G ≤ Sn be a primitive group of order |G| ≥ n1+log2 n where n is
greater than some absolute constant. Then G has a normal subgroup N of index ≤ n such
(t)

Moreover, N and the system of imprimitivity in question can be found in polynomial time.

highlights.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson (PDF p. 94) — **Line 4 of Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson** (§11.3, line 5048): the routine returns a *minimal* system of imprimitivity — at least two blocks, and the blocks are maximal (§11.1).
highlights.prose:
Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson
Input: group G ≤ S(Ω), strings x, y : Ω → Σ
Output: IsoG (x, y) or updated Ω, G, x, y, G transitive, with set B of blocks on which G acts
as Johnson group G ≤ S(B)
1. if G ≤ Aut(x) then
if x = y then return IsoG (x, y) = G, exit
else return IsoG (x, y) = ∅, exit
2. if |G| < C0 for some absolute constant C0 then compute IsoG (x, y) by brute force, exit
3. if G intransitive then apply Chain Rule
4. (: G transitive :) Find minimal block system B. Let m = |B|. Let G ≤ S(B) be the
induced G-action on B and N the kernel of the G → G epimorphism (: G is a primitive
group :)
5. if |G| < m1+log2 m then reduce G to N via imprimitive Luks reduction

highlights.prose:
Definition 12.0.3. A subcoset of a group G is a coset of a subgroup. Let H ≤ G be groups
and τ ∈ G. We say that the subset S ⊆ Hτ is a set of coset generators of Hτ if Hτ is the
smallest subcoset of G containing S. (Note that any intersection of subcosets of G is either
empty or a subcoset; so every subset of G generates a subcoset of G.)

G → S(Γ) a giant representation, where |Γ| = m > max{8, 2 + log2 n}. Given these data and
the strings x, y : Ω → Σ, we can achieve the following by recursively calling ≤ 6k instances
of String Isomorphism with window size ≤ n/k for some m ≤ k ≤ n, at polynomial cost per
instance:
(i) decide whether φ maps IsoG (x, y) onto a giant coset, i. e., IsoG (x, y)φ ≥ A(Γ)τ for some
τ ∈ S(Γ);
(ii) if the answer is affirmative, find IsoG (x, y).

G → S(Γ) a giant representation, where |Γ| = m > max{8, 2 + log2 n}. Given these data and
the strings x, y : Ω → Σ, we can achieve the following by recursively calling ≤ 6k instances
of String Isomorphism with window size ≤ n/k for some m ≤ k ≤ n, at polynomial cost per
instance:
(i) decide whether φ maps AutG (x) onto a giant, i. e., AutG (x)φ ≥ A(Γ);
(iii) if the answer is affirmative, find IsoG (x, y).

Corollary 12.0.10 (TopAction4). Let G ≤ S(Ω) be a transitive permutation group and
φ : G → S(Γ) a giant representation where |Γ| = m ≥ max{16, 4 + 2 log2 n}. Let x, y : Ω → Σ
be strings. Assume Γ has a canonical coloring with respect to x with a color class C of size
|C| > m/2 such that the restriction of AutG (x)φ to C is a giant (includes A(C)). Then we
can find IsoG (x, y) by recursively calling ≤ 6k instances of String Isomorphism with window
size ≤ n/k for some |C| ≤ k ≤ n, plus a number of instances of total size ≤ n and maximum
size ≤ 2n/3.

Notation 13.1.1. Recall that for a subgroup L ≤ G and a subset A ⊆ Γ we write LA to
denote the setwise stabilizer of A in L with respect to the representation φ|L : L → S(Γ).
We say that A is L-invariant if LA = L. We write ψA : GA → S(A) for the map that restricts
the G φ -action to A. If A is L-invariant then LA := LψA is the restriction of L φ to A. In
particular, ψΓ = φ and LΓ = L φ .

highlights.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 13.1.3 (Local certificates) (PDF p. 101) — The entry of one certificate run is the paper's certificate of fullness or of non-fullness, by Theorem 13.1.3.
highlights.prose:
Theorem 13.1.3 (Local certificates). Let T ⊆ Γ where |T | = t. We refer to T as our “test
set.” Assume max{8, 2 + log2 n} < t ≤ m/10. By making ≤ t!n2 calls to String Isomorphism
problems on domains of size ≤ n/t and performing t! poly(n) computation we can decide
whether T is full and
(a) if T is full, find a certificate K(T ) ≤ AutG (x) of fullness;
(b) if T is not full, find a certificate M (T ) ≤ S(T ) of non-fullness.
The families {(T, K(T )) : T ∈ F(x)} and {(T, M (T )) : T ∈ F(x)} are canonical.

highlights.prose:
Theorem 13.2.1 (AggregateCertificates). Let φ : G → S(Γ) be a giant representation,
where G ≤ S(Ω), |Ω| = n, and |Γ| = m. Let max{8, 2 + log2 n} < t < m/10. Then, at a
multiplicative cost of mO(t) , we can either find a canonical colored 4/5-partition of Γ or find
a canonically embedded t-ary relational structure with relative symmetry defect ≥ 1/2 on Γ,
or reduce the determination of IsoG (x, y) to nO(1) instances of size ≤ 2n/3.

where G ≤ S(Ω), |Ω| = n, and |Γ| = m. Let max{8, 2 + log2 n} < t < m/10. Then, at a
multiplicative cost of mO(t) , we can either find a canonical colored 4/5-partition of Γ or find
a canonically embedded t-ary relational structure with relative symmetry defect ≥ 1/2 on Γ,
or reduce the determination of IsoG (x, y) to nO(1) instances of size ≤ 2n/3.

Input: group G ≤ S(Ω), strings x, y : Ω → Σ
Output: IsoG (x, y)
1. Apply Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson (Luks reductions, Sec. 11.3)
(: The rest of this algorithm constitutes the ProcessJohnsonAction routine announced
in Sec. 11.3)
2. (: G is transitive, G-action G on blocks is Johnson group isomorphic to Sm or Am :)
set ℓ = (log n)3
if m ≤ ℓ then apply imprimitive Luks reduction to reduce to kernel of the G-action on
the blocks (brute force on small primitive group G, multiplicative cost ℓ! :)

Input: group G ≤ S(Ω), strings x, y : Ω → Σ
Output: IsoG (x, y)

(: The rest of this algorithm constitutes the ProcessJohnsonAction routine announced
in Sec. 11.3)

the blocks (brute force on small primitive group G, multiplicative cost ℓ! :)
